issues.legal_issue: A Domestic Incident Report is not a prerequisite to a Magistrate entertaining an application for relief under the domestic violence legislation, although a report received from a Protection Officer or service provider must be considered.
material_facts: The aggrieved person filed her application directly before the Magistrate, without a Domestic Incident Report from a Protection Officer or service provider.
The High Court held that the Magistrate could not grant relief because the application was not accompanied by a Domestic Incident Report.
issues.conclusion: The Magistrate may entertain and decide an application even when no Domestic Incident Report has been filed; if such a report is received from a Protection Officer or service provider, the Magistrate must take it into consideration before passing an order.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(e), 8, 9, 10 and 12(1) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Rule 5 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Rules, 2006, and Section 23 show that an aggrieved person may apply directly or through another person, and the proviso to Section 12(1) requires consideration of a report when one is received, not that a report be obtained in every case. A contrary reading would defeat the main provision and the Act’s remedial purpose. The Court relied on the principles governing provisos in Ishverlal Thakorelal Almaula v. Motibhai Nagjibhai, Kaviraj Pandit Durga Dutt Sharma v. Navaratna Pharmaceutical Laboratories, Kedarnath Jute Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer, Dattatraya Govind Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra, S. Sundaram Pillai v. V.R. Pattabiraman, M. Pentiah v. Muddala Veeramallappa and Superintendent & Remembrancer of Legal Affairs v. Abani Maity. It overruled Rama Singh v. Maya Singh and Ravi Dutta v. Kiran Dutta, and affirmed the consistent approach in decisions including Shambhu Prasad Singh v. Manjari.

rule.if: domestic_violence_application and ((applicant_applied_without_support_service and not incident_report_received) or incident_report_received)

predicates.domestic_violence_application: A woman or someone acting on her behalf sought relief from a Magistrate for alleged domestic violence.
predicates.applicant_applied_without_support_servic: The applicant presented the application without using a Protection Officer or service provider to submit it.
predicates.incident_report_received: The Magistrate received a Domestic Incident Report from a Protection Officer or service provider.

issues.definition: When a domestic-violence application is made directly without a report, or a report is received, the report is not a prerequisite to the Magistrate entertaining the application.

issues.legal_issue: An aggrieved woman need not actually reside with the respondent when the alleged domestic violence occurs or when she seeks relief, if she has the relevant domestic relationship and right to reside in a shared household.
material_facts: The aggrieved person was married to the respondent’s son, who died shortly after the marriage.
She alleged that the respondent and other family members harassed and mentally tortured her, causing her to leave the matrimonial home, and that she was living elsewhere when she applied for relief.
The lower courts denied relief in part because they found that she had not shared a household with the respondents.
issues.conclusion: Actual residence with the respondent at the time of the alleged violence is not mandatory; a woman with the right to reside in a shared household may seek relief under the Act even if she is not actually living there.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(a), 2(f), 2(s), 17 and 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, read together, protect a woman in a qualifying domestic relationship and do not make actual co-residence at the time of violence a condition for relief. Section 17(1) gives every woman in a domestic relationship a right to reside in a shared household irrespective of her legal or beneficial interest in it; that right is not confined to actual residence. The Court relied on Juveria Abdul Majid Patni v. Atif Iqbal Mansoori, Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja, Vandhana v. T. Srikanth and Smt. Bharati Naik v. Shri Ravi Ramnath Halarnkar.

rule.if: domestic_violence_application and qualifying_domestic_relationship and alleged_domestic_violence and right_to_reside_in_shared_household and not residing_with_respondent_when_violence_occurred

predicates.domestic_violence_application: A woman or someone acting on her behalf sought relief from a Magistrate for alleged domestic violence.
predicates.qualifying_domestic_relationship: The woman is or has been related to the respondent through a legally recognized domestic relationship and has lived in, or has the right to reside in, a shared household.
predicates.alleged_domestic_violence: The woman alleged conduct by the respondent amounting to domestic violence.
predicates.right_to_reside_in_shared_household: The woman had a right to reside in a household shared by virtue of the domestic relationship, regardless of ownership or other legal interest.
predicates.residing_with_respondent_when_violence_o: The woman was actually residing with the respondent when the alleged domestic violence occurred.

issues.definition: If a woman with a qualifying domestic relationship and a right to reside in a shared household alleges domestic violence, she may seek relief even when she was not actually living with the respondent when it occurred.

issues.legal_issue: A domestic relationship need not still exist when an application for relief is filed if the alleged domestic violence relates to the relationship or is later inflicted on account of it.
material_facts: The aggrieved person’s husband died shortly after their marriage, before she filed her application for relief.
She alleged that her in-laws harassed her after his death and that she was forced to leave the matrimonial home.
The lower courts treated the absence of a current domestic relationship and the fact that she was living separately as grounds to deny relief.
issues.conclusion: A woman may apply under the Act even if the domestic relationship has ended by the time of filing, provided the alleged domestic violence relates to the period of that relationship or is later inflicted on account of it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(a) and 2(f) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, define an aggrieved person and domestic relationship to include past relationships; the phrase “have at any point of time, lived together” does not require the relationship to subsist when the application is made. Violence must, however, relate to the domestic relationship. The Court relied on Juveria Abdul Majid Patni v. Atif Iqbal Mansoori, which recognized claims based on past domestic relationships and later conduct related to them; Krishna Bhattacharjee v. Sarathi Choudhury, which held that judicial separation does not end the domestic relationship; Saraswathy v. Babu; and V.D. Bhanot v. Savita Bhanot.

rule.if: domestic_violence_application and past_qualifying_domestic_relationship and not relationship_subsisting_when_filed and alleged_violence_related_to_relationship

predicates.domestic_violence_application: A woman or someone acting on her behalf sought relief from a Magistrate for alleged domestic violence.
predicates.past_qualifying_domestic_relationship: The woman and respondent had previously lived together in a shared household while related through a qualifying domestic relationship.
predicates.relationship_subsisting_when_filed: The qualifying domestic relationship still existed when the woman filed her application.
predicates.alleged_violence_related_to_relationship: The alleged domestic violence occurred during the domestic relationship or was later inflicted on account of that relationship.

issues.definition: A woman may apply after a qualifying domestic relationship has ended when the alleged violence is related to that relationship.
